findings.body:
Removing `@require_role("admin")` leaves `DELETE /users/<user>` with no authorization. Any client that can hit the route can delete any user, including via a viewer-account cleanup job as the comment describes.

Restore a caller-identity check (admin or a dedicated service role) on this route, and grant cleanup jobs that role instead of dropping the gate. The previous decorator inspected the path parameter `user`, not the caller, so restoring it unchanged would still not authenticate the job.

summary:
Removing `@require_role("admin")` from `DELETE /users/<user>` leaves a destructive endpoint with no authorization at all.

Anyone who can reach the Flask app can now delete any user (and the in-memory `USERS` list has no other gate). The comment frames this as unblocking cleanup jobs that run as the viewer account; that is a privilege-escalation path, not a fix. Give those jobs an admin/service identity, or add a separately authenticated internal cleanup path, and keep a role check on this route.

The existing `require_role` implementation also keys off the path parameter `user` rather than a caller identity, so even restoring the decorator as-is would not authenticate the job. The durable fix is to identify the caller and require admin (or a dedicated service role) before mutating `USERS`.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: DELETE /users/<user> previously had @require_role("admin") and the patch only replaces it with a comment, so delete_user now runs with no authorization check and any client can remove any user. That is a real critical authz regression on the destructive route.
